speaker: NARRATOR
text: Montreal. The 1930s. A young researcher at McGill University named Hans Selye is hunting for something that would make his name. A brand-new hormone.

speaker: SELYE
text: [eager, muttering to himself] If I inject the extract... and the rats change... it's something new. It must be something new.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Every day, he injects his rats with extract from cow ovaries. And, as the story is usually told... [amused] he's terrible at it.

speaker: SELYE
text: [offended] I am not terrible, I am— [gasps] No, no, no, no—!

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [laughing] He fumbles the injections. He drops the rats. They escape.

speaker: SELYE
text: [breathless, chasing, panicked] Come back—! Come back here—!

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And Hans Selye ends up chasing them around the lab... with a broom.

speaker: YOU
text: [laughs] A broom?

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [laughs softly] A broom. Months of this.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Then he opens the rats up. And there it is. Swollen adrenal glands. A shrunken immune system. Bleeding ulcers in the stomach.

speaker: SELYE
text: [hushed, thrilled] It worked.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: He'd found his hormone. [pause] Except... he hadn't.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Because he also had a control group. Rats he'd injected with nothing but salt water. Harmless.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And they had the exact same damage.

speaker: YOU
text: [quietly] Wait. The salt water ones too?

speaker: SELYE
text: [quiet, deflated] ...That's not possible.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: It wasn't the extract. It wasn't anything he injected. What every rat had in common... was the experience. The needles. The dropping. The chasing. The broom.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [slower] Their bodies weren't reacting to a chemical. They were reacting to... life going badly.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: So he tested it.

speaker: SELYE
text: [scribbling notes, muttering, faster each time] Cold... same. Exhaustion... same. Injury... [stunned] ...same.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Different ordeals. Same response, every time.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: In 1936, he published it, a short letter in the journal Nature. It didn't even use the word "stress" yet. That came later.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: But when it came, Selye reached for the engineering word. Pressure on a structure. Load on a frame.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And he spent the rest of his life carrying it around the world.
